I ran the numbers twice before I let myself believe them. The relay had been quiet
for two days, and the console at Sol threw up the same answer either way, which is
the sort of thing that stops being reassuring after the third pass.

"You could just accept it," said the desk, which had opinions.

I did not accept it. Somebody had moved the chart tables again, and I spent the
better part of the morning putting them back, which is the kind of work that lets
a person avoid a decision honestly.

The truth was that Vela had gone quiet and I did not know why. Not knowing why is
a specific flavour of dread. You cannot chase it, you cannot log it, and you
certainly cannot send a query and wait twenty-four years for the shrug to come
back.

So I did what a cartographer does. I drew the boundary of my ignorance and I made
it precise. Everything inside the line, I knew. Everything outside it, I marked
honestly as dark, and I signed the chart, and I filed it.

Outside the port the traffic lanes were doing their slow arithmetic. Order, even
somebody else's. I let it hold me up for a minute and then I went back inside and
started the third pass.
